sentences.text: In the second week Avôlo let Rafael sit at the wheel.
He showed him how to center a lump of clay — how to place it firmly, how to push down with both hands as it spun, how to feel when it was true.
It was much harder than it looked.
Rafael's first lump wobbled and flew off the wheel.
His second lump collapsed.
His third lump would not center — it kept trying to spin off to one side.
"You are fighting it," Avôlo said, patient.
"Stop pushing so hard.
Let your hands move with it.
Do not try to force it into the shape you want.
Feel where it wants to be, and guide it there."
Rafael slowed down.
He breathed.
He tried again.
On the fourth try, the lump centered.
It sat still on the wheel, spinning, but not moving from its axis.
It was — he felt it — a completely different feeling.
Almost as if the wheel had disappeared and there was only him and the clay and a quiet space between them.
Avôlo said, softly, "Yes.
Now.
Do not lose it.
Just breathe.
Feel that?
That is what centered feels like.
Now — thumbs.
In the middle.
Push down."
Rafael pushed his thumbs into the top of the spinning lump.
He opened it up — a small dip that widened as the wheel spun.
Then, with his fingers on the outside and his other hand on the inside, he began — very slowly — to draw the walls up.
This was harder than centering.
If he pulled unevenly, the walls got thin on one side and the whole pot leaned.
If he pulled too fast, the walls tore.
If he pulled too slowly, the clay got too dry and cracked.
Twice his first attempt failed.
On the third try, he got a small crooked bowl — maybe seven centimeters wide, five tall, walls uneven.
It stayed standing when he stopped the wheel.
He looked at Avôlo.
Avôlo was looking at the bowl with a small smile.
He said, "That is your first bowl, Rafael.
It is not a pretty bowl.
But it is a real bowl.
You made it.
Now we cut it off the wheel and set it aside.
Tomorrow it will be dry enough to trim.
Then we fire it.
Then it is yours."
For the rest of the week Rafael worked at the wheel every morning.
He got better slowly.
His pots stopped collapsing.
His walls got more even.
On the fifth day, he made a bowl that Avôlo said was actually acceptable — not just beginner acceptable, but real acceptable.
Rafael was proud.
He was also — he noticed — tired.
Working with clay took much more of him than he had expected.
His arms hurt.
His back hurt.
His mind was quiet in a way he was not used to.
When he stopped working, at the end of a morning, and went outside to the courtyard for water, he felt like he had been somewhere else, and he was slowly coming back.
"Avôlo," he asked, one afternoon, when they were sitting in the courtyard eating oranges.
"Why do you love this.
You have done it for fifty years.
Do you not get tired of it." Avôlo peeled his orange slowly.
He said, "Rafael.
Have I ever told you why I became a potter." "No," said Rafael.
"Not properly." Avôlo said, "My mother died when I was your age.
Ten years old.
She was sick for six months.
In those six months I was — I did not know what to do with myself.
There was too much feeling inside me.
My father was a potter, though not a very good one.
He put me in the workshop with him.
He gave me clay.
He said — do not shape anything.
Just — hold it.
Just — hold it, and be with it, and let it hold what you cannot say.
I sat with a lump of clay every afternoon for six months.
When my mother died, the lump had been shaped by my hands into a small crooked bowl, though I did not remember shaping it.
My father fired it.
He gave it to me.
I still have it."
Rafael was quiet.
He said, "Is that why you make so many bowls, Avôlo.
Because your first one was a bowl." Avôlo laughed a small laugh.
He said, "No.
I make many bowls because people need bowls.
But — maybe a little bit yes.
A bowl is a container.
It holds what you cannot say.
A bowl is a hand cupped, always.
Every bowl I make is — someone will use it.
Soup.
Fruit.
Coins.
A ring taken off at night.
Every bowl holds something.
That is why I love it.
Every bowl is going to hold a small piece of some person's life.
And I made the bowl.
That is a small immortality." He looked at Rafael.
"Some day, Rafael, one of your bowls will hold soup for your grandchildren.
You will not remember making it.
But it will be there.
That is what a potter does."
On the second-to-last day, they fired Rafael's pots.

Rafael had made five in the second week that Avôlo said were worth firing — three small bowls, one small cup, and a very small odd-shaped thing that was supposed to be a vase but had come out looking like a small squat mushroom.
They loaded them into the kiln.
Avôlo showed Rafael how to set the fire.
The kiln was small and wood-fired, in the old way.
It took eight hours to reach the right temperature.
They tended it together all day.
Rafael put pieces of wood in when Avôlo told him to.
He watched the color of the flame — Avôlo said the color told you the temperature better than any thermometer.
That night when the kiln had cooled — they had let it cool overnight, and opened it in the morning — they took out the finished pots.
They were transformed.
The dull grey clay had become a warm terra-cotta orange.
Rafael's odd little vase-mushroom was beautiful now — the color made it look intentional.
His three bowls were solid and real.
His cup had a small crack that Avôlo said was fine — cracks happen sometimes, and this one would not affect the use.
Rafael held one of his bowls in both hands.
It was small and warm and honest.
He said, "I made this." Avôlo said, "You did."
